problem: Existing social navigation methods treat pedestrians as obstacles or rely on hand-crafted features, known goals, full-accuracy sensing and global maps, and none handle a robot travelling together with a human companion.
motivation: Assistive and companion robots must travel alongside a person through crowds, which requires joint collision avoidance with pedestrians and staying close to the companion. Hand-crafted or demonstration-based models are environment- and hardware-specific and ignore sensor noise and limited field of view. Real pedestrian trajectory datasets can instead be replayed as a safe simulator for RL.
key_idea: Role Playing Learning: replay real-world pedestrian trajectory datasets as a simulator in which a robot with a stochastic NN policy plays itself as a pedestrian's companion, and train the policy end-to-end with a partially observable TRPO (PO-TRPO).
insight: Learning from replayed real trajectories with noisy, limited-FoV observations yields a map-free policy that transfers to a real robot. In simulation, the RVO baseline mostly loses its companion (LC 47%), showing that pure collision avoidance cannot do companion following, whereas the learned policy reaches the goal 77% of the time. Mixing SCN and no-companion episodes (50/50, with a synthesized companion) makes one policy work in both settings. No ablations are provided, so these are supported only by comparison against RVO.
method: POMDP formulation: state has goal distance/angle, current action, the 3 nearest pedestrians, the companion, and 9 compact obstacle variables (front, plus closest/farthest on each side); observation adds noise and FoV limits (±2π/3), with noise σ=0.01·distance
Reward: +10000 for reaching the goal (within 0.8 m); -10000 for collision or straying (companion distance ≥2 m); -10|vR| per step to discourage turning

RPL simulator: 8 environments built from ETH, Hotel, MC, Zara01-03 and UCY01/03 trajectories with binary maps used only to simulate sensing; the robot starts at a trajectory start, goal is its end, and the companion is a truncated trajectory (SCN mode, p=0.5) or a synthesized fixed companion at 0.8 m
Policy network: MLP feature net (256, 64 Tanh) -> LSTM (64) -> mean of a diagonal Gaussian over [vT, vR] with σ decaying 0.5 -> 0.05 over 100 iterations

PO-TRPO: TRPO with observation-conditioned policy and importance-sampled surrogate, GAE (γ=0.995, λ=0.96), value net (256, 64, 16), conjugate gradient, KL step ε=0.01/σ, batch size 50000, implemented in rllab
Real deployment: Turtlebot2 with Hokuyo URG-04LX, leg tracker for pedestrians, UWB localization for the companion and goal, laptop running the policy at 10 Hz

setting.backbone: MLP + LSTM stochastic Gaussian policy (trained from scratch with PO-TRPO)
setting.training_data: Simulated episodes from 7 real pedestrian trajectory datasets (ETH held out), 1200 iterations x 50000 steps; 148-434 trajectories per environment
setting.observation: 2D laser-derived relative distances/angles of pedestrians, companion and obstacles (FoV ±120°, noisy), plus goal distance/angle and previous action
setting.simulator: custom trajectory-replay simulator built on rllab
setting.privileged: none at test time (binary maps only used to simulate sensing in sim; UWB localization of companion and goal in real experiments)

results: In the held-out ETH simulation, the policy reaches the goal 77% in SCN vs 29.7% for an RVO planner that had perfect obstacle maps and velocity information (RVO lost its companion 47% of the time). Without a companion it achieves 84% vs 80% for RVO. On a real Turtlebot the robot keeps a mean max companion distance of 1.05 m, close to a human's 1 m, and behaves cooperatively in a narrow corridor.
limitations: Evaluated only on a single held-out dataset (ETH) against a single baseline (RVO), with no ablations
Pedestrians in the simulator replay fixed recorded trajectories and do not react to the robot, and real experiments rely on UWB localization and are small-scale (10 runs)
Robot collides with pedestrians frequently in simulation (HP 9.6-13.7%), and the real robot keeps a smaller pedestrian distance than humans
